name: Perthes' disease
aliases: idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children

reference.source: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
clinicalPearls: An idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children, typically presenting between about 4 and 8 years and more common in boys
Presents with a limp and hip, groin, or referred knee pain, often intermittent, with restricted abduction and internal rotation of the hip
Knee pain in a child can be referred from the hip, so the hip must always be examined in a limping child
Early radiographs may be normal; later changes include increased femoral head density, fragmentation, flattening, and eventual remodelling
The key aims are to relieve symptoms, maintain hip movement, and keep the femoral head 'contained' within the acetabulum so it remodels into a congruent, spherical shape
Younger children with more remaining growth and greater remodelling potential generally have a better prognosis than older children
Treatment ranges from observation, activity restriction, and physiotherapy to containment by bracing or surgery (femoral or pelvic osteotomy) in more severe or older cases
Bilateral or atypical presentations should prompt consideration of alternative diagnoses such as skeletal dysplasia or hypothyroidism
reference.pathophysiology: Perthes' disease results from a temporary interruption of the blood supply to the immature femoral head epiphysis, causing avascular necrosis. The precise trigger is unknown but the epiphysis undergoes a sequence of ischaemic necrosis, followed by fragmentation and resorption of dead bone, then reossification and remodelling as revascularisation occurs. During the biologically 'plastic' necrotic and fragmentation phases the softened femoral head is vulnerable to deformation under load, and can flatten and enlarge (coxa magna) or become incongruent if not well contained within the acetabulum. The ultimate shape of the healed head, and hence long-term function, depends on how well sphericity and containment are preserved through this self-limiting but prolonged process.
additionalDifferentials: Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis of the hip
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (in older children)
Skeletal dysplasia or epiphyseal dysplasia (especially if bilateral)
Hypothyroidism and avascular necrosis from other causes (e.g. sickle cell disease, steroids)
additionalInvestigations: Anteroposterior and frog-lateral radiographs of both hips to assess and stage the changes
MRI for early detection before radiographic changes appear and to assess the extent of necrosis
Clinical assessment of hip range of movement, particularly abduction and internal rotation
Investigations to exclude infection or inflammatory arthritis when the presentation is acute
Consideration of bilateral or systemic workup (e.g. thyroid function, skeletal survey) if presentation is atypical or bilateral
redFlags: Fever, systemic upset, and an acutely irritable hip suggesting septic arthritis requiring urgent exclusion
Bilateral or atypical disease suggesting skeletal dysplasia or an underlying systemic cause
Marked loss of hip movement and femoral head extrusion indicating a head at risk of permanent deformity
An older child at presentation, associated with a poorer remodelling capacity
reference.prognosis: The disease is self-limiting and many younger children with limited head involvement remodel to a near-normal, congruent hip; however, older children, extensive necrosis, and a poorly contained or deformed femoral head are associated with residual incongruity and an increased risk of premature hip osteoarthritis in adulthood.
pitfalls: Attributing a child's knee pain to the knee and failing to examine the hip
Assuming a normal early radiograph excludes the disease and missing early presentation on MRI
Not distinguishing Perthes' disease from septic arthritis in the acutely painful hip
Overlooking bilateral involvement that should prompt evaluation for an underlying systemic disorder
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Relieve symptoms with simple analgesia, activity modification and physiotherapy to preserve hip range of movement
Maintain femoral head containment within the acetabulum by preserving abduction and internal rotation, using physiotherapy and, in selected cases, abduction bracing
Protected weight-bearing and traction during painful active phases to reduce load on the softened epiphysis
Surgical containment with femoral varus or pelvic acetabular osteotomy for older children or those with extensive involvement or loss of containment
Serial radiographic monitoring through the fragmentation and reossification phases to track sphericity and containment
Coordinate orthopaedic and physiotherapy care, tailoring intensity to age and extent of head involvement
Long-term surveillance for residual deformity and premature hip osteoarthritis
